sections.h: Judith: "king of the Assyrians" who would be god
sections.b: Judith opens with "Nebuchadnezzar, who ruled over the Assyrians in Nineveh" (Judith 1:1), a title no reader of Kings could take at face value: Nineveh fell before his reign, and he was king of Babylon. In Judith he defeats the Median king Arphaxad, swears revenge on the nations that ignored his summons (Judith 1:7–12), and sends Holofernes to make all nations worship him alone (Judith 3:8). His officer asks, "Who is god except Nebuchadnezzar?" (Judith 6:2). Most scholars, Catholic and Protestant, read this Nebuchadnezzar as a composite of Israel's great enemies, Babylon, Assyria and, for the first readers, Antiochus IV. Older Catholic writers tried to identify him with Ashurbanipal or another king under a throne name (Hugh Pope, 1910).

common: Most scholars read Judith's Nebuchadnezzar as a deliberately unhistorical figure who stands for every empire that threatened Israel.
uncommon: Older Catholic writers such as Vigouroux identified Judith's Nebuchadnezzar with Ashurbanipal of Assyria, placing the story under King Manasseh.

sections.b: Achior's speech (Judith 5:5–21) is the longest summary of Israel's history in the book and follows the pattern of the creeds in Deuteronomy 26:5–9, Joshua 24:2–13 and Nehemiah 9: Chaldean origins, a sojourn in Canaan and Egypt, slavery, the plagues, the sea, the wilderness and the conquest, then sin, exile and return. It adds that Abraham's family was driven out for refusing the gods of Chaldea (Judith 5:8), a tradition known from later Jewish sources. Its rule, that Israel is safe while it does not sin (Judith 5:17–21), is the theology of Deuteronomy 28.

sections.h: Before Judith appears: the empire and the town (chapters 1–7)
sections.b: Judith does not appear until chapter 8. The first half of the book sets the stage: a king who claims to be god (Judith 3:8; Judith 6:2), a general who conquers the known world (Judith 2:14–3:10), a people newly returned from exile who repent in sackcloth (Judith 4:1–15), an Ammonite who tells the truth about Israel's God (Judith 5:5–21), and a small hill town, Bethulia, whose water is cut off (Judith 7:1–22). It ends with the elders' promise to surrender if God has not helped in five days (Judith 7:30–31), the deadline Judith will rebuke (Judith 8:11–17). Scholars note that the two halves mirror each other: the great king's council and the town's assembly, his boasts and her prayers, his army and her single hand.

sections.b: Though set under Nebuchadnezzar, Judith is full of Persian touches. Holofernes and the eunuch Bagoas (Judith 2:4; Judith 12:11) bear names known from the army of Artaxerxes III in the 340s BC (Diodorus, Library of History 16 and 31). The coastal rulers are "satraps" (Judith 5:2), Nebuchadnezzar demands "earth and water" as Persian kings did (Judith 2:7; Herodotus, Histories 6.48), and the people have returned from exile and reconsecrated the Temple (Judith 4:3), as they did under Persia (Ezra 1–6). Some scholars date the book's origins to the Persian period for these reasons; most think the author borrowed Persian colour for a Hasmonean-era story.

sections.b: Judith twice says the people had only lately come up from captivity and reconsecrated the Temple (Judith 4:3; Judith 5:18–19). Achior's speech reads the exile as the result of Israel's sin and the return as the result of its repentance, as Deuteronomy, Kings and Ezra do (Deuteronomy 30:1–5; 2 Kings 17:7–23; Ezra 9:7–9). The setting, under a Nebuchadnezzar who was in fact the cause of the exile, is one of the book's deliberate historical riddles.

sections.h: Judith: Abraham leaves the gods of Chaldea
sections.b: Achior tells Holofernes that Israel's ancestors were Chaldeans who would not follow the gods of their fathers, worshiped "the God of heaven," and were thrown out by their kin (Judith 5:6–8). The Bible says only that Terah's family "served other gods" (Joshua 24:2) and that God brought Abram out of Ur of the Chaldeans (Genesis 15:7). Judith is one of the earliest witnesses to the later Jewish story of Abraham's break with idolatry, known from Jubilees 12 and Genesis Rabbah 38:13.

sections.h: Judith: "as long as they did not sin"
sections.b: Achior gives Holofernes the rule of Deuteronomy in a sentence: as long as Israel did not sin, good things were theirs; when they turned away, they were beaten and exiled (Judith 5:17–18). So, he says, find out if they are sinning now (Judith 5:20–21). The people of Bethulia read their own suffering the same way, as punishment for sin (Judith 7:28). Judith will qualify the rule: suffering may be God's testing rather than his punishment (Judith 8:25–27).

sections.h: Judith: a whole nation in sackcloth
sections.b: When Holofernes approaches, all Israel fasts: men, women, children, foreigners, hired workers, slaves and cattle wear sackcloth, the people lie face down before the Temple, and the altar itself is wrapped in sackcloth (Judith 4:9–15). "The Lord heard their cry and saw their distress" (Judith 4:13). The scene echoes the fasts of Nineveh (Jonah 3:5–9), of Joel (Joel 2:12–17) and of Esther (Esther 4:1–3, 4:16).

sections.h: Judith: the Temple newly made holy
sections.b: Judea's first fear is for the Temple (Judith 4:2), which had lately been reconsecrated after it was defiled (Judith 4:3). The people pray that the holy place not be profaned (Judith 4:12), and the priests offer the regular burnt offering in sackcloth (Judith 4:14). Many scholars hear behind Judith 4:3 the cleansing of the Temple by Judas Maccabeus in 164 BC (1 Maccabees 4:36–59).

Holofernes is ordered "to destroy all the gods of the land, so that all the nations would worship Nebuchadnezzar alone, and every language and tribe would call on him as god" (Judith 3:8). The demand recalls Daniel 3 and, for the first readers, the god-king claims of the Seleucid ruler Antiochus IV. No real Assyrian or Babylonian king made it.

Holofernes' question (Judith 6:2) is the hinge of the book, and its answer is Deuteronomy 32:39. Judith's prayer asks God to make every nation know "that you are the God of all power and strength, and that no one but you shields the race of Israel" (Judith 9:14).

sections.h: Judith: echoes of Balak and Balaam
sections.b: The scenes in Holofernes' camp echo Numbers 22–24. Moabites are among his advisers; he sneers at "this people that came out of Egypt," as Balak did (Judith 6:5; Numbers 22:5); the Israelites fear the army will "lick clean" the land, Moab's words (Judith 7:4; Numbers 22:4); and Achior, mocked as a prophet for hire (Judith 6:2), can only tell the truth about Israel, as Balaam could only bless.

sections.h: Judith as a story for the Maccabean age
sections.b: Most scholars date Judith to about 150–100 BC and read its first half against the Maccabean war: a king who demands worship (Judith 3:8), a Temple newly reconsecrated (Judith 4:3), a nation fasting in sackcloth (Judith 4:9–15; 1 Maccabees 3:46–54), a high priest and council of elders who direct the defense (Judith 4:6–8), and old neighbors such as Edom, Ammon and Moab among the enemy (Judith 5:2; Judith 7:8).

sections.h: Judith: the council of elders and the town elders
sections.b: In Judith the high priest rules with "the council of elders of all the people of Israel, who sat in Jerusalem" (Judith 4:8), the Greek gerousia known from the Persian and Hellenistic periods. In Bethulia, the town elders gather with the rulers (Judith 6:16; Judith 7:23) and agree to Uzziah's five-day promise (Judith 7:30–31), which Judith will rebuke (Judith 8:11).

sections.h: Judith: the descendants of Esau at the siege
sections.b: The "descendants of Esau" advise Holofernes to take Bethulia's water and camp on the hills around it (Judith 7:8–18), as Edom was remembered for joining Jerusalem's enemies (Psalm 137:7; Obadiah 1:10–14). For the first readers Edom was Idumea, which John Hyrcanus conquered in the late 100s BC (the date is debated).

sections.h: Judith: five days to wait for God
sections.b: Uzziah tells the dying town, "Let us endure five more days": God will surely turn his mercy toward them, and if not, he will surrender (Judith 7:30–31). The book treats the promise as a lapse of faith, a test set for God like Israel's at Massah (Exodus 17:7; Deuteronomy 6:16), and Judith rebukes it (Judith 8:11–17).

sections.h: Judith: Bethulia in the hills of Samaria
sections.b: Judith sets its siege in the northern hill country, between Esdraelon and Dothan (Judith 4:4–6; Judith 7:3), in the old territory of Samaria, though the people there are loyal to Jerusalem's high priest. For the first readers this matched the Hasmonean push north, when John Hyrcanus destroyed the Samaritan temple on Mount Gerizim and the town of Shechem, in the late 100s BC.

sections.h: Judith: the high priest at war
sections.b: In Judith the high priest Joakim, not a king, organizes the defense: he writes to Bethulia to hold the passes (Judith 4:6–7) and leads the priests in sackcloth at the altar (Judith 4:14–15). The picture fits a priestly state like Hasmonean Judea, whose high priests were also its generals.
